compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
The premise is aligned conditions: the same day, the same aisle, the same clear-width requirement, the same media slot, the same supervisor, the same temporary staffing. If one person is the site lead and the other is helping for an hour, their different access and responsibilities may explain what they do.

Each row names what each type may take first in the same event and states which axis it mainly sits on. Both types can use both approaches; the table describes which is taken first more often, is not a scale of ability, and cannot be used as a typing sheet.

| The same event (one fair, the same authority and constraints) | ENTJ: the basis more likely attended to | ESTP: the basis more likely attended to | Which axis this row mainly sits on |

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In this fictional example, a queue blocks the main aisle on the first morning of a trade fair, and a media slot is scheduled for eleven. Two staff members are called to help. Both can stay engaged and follow the venue’s procedures. That response shows what they did in this situation.

The resemblance comes from the shared E and T: attention and energy turn more toward what is happening outside; and judgement more often wants a figure that can be put on the table and applied to everyone equally (throughput, waiting time, clear aisle width). That describes direction and standard, not who is more decisive, and not who understands the floor better.

The difference sits on two preferences. On sourcing, ENTJ more often takes the connections and direction of the information: where this queue will block in ten minutes, which step becomes the bottleneck first; ESTP more often takes the observable facts and past experience: which action people are stuck on right now, what happened last time this was changed. On the outward side, ENTJ more often settles the arrangement and the conclusion, and ESTP more often keeps options and adjusts while working.

### Changing the floor: resources or actions

The same fictional scene: the stand has pushed its queue into the main aisle, the aisle has to keep the clear width the fire rules require, there is a media slot at eleven, the temporary staff only arrived that morning, and both are proposing within their authority.

One proposal focuses on staffing and timing: estimate throughput per unit of time, release people in time slots, add a guiding position at the entrance, and put one person at the end of the queue to announce the expected wait. This proposal asks how many people can take part at a time, when to admit them and where to place staff.

Another proposal looks for a specific step that is slowing the queue: walk into the middle of the queue to see which step people are stuck on, and if the bottleneck is waiting for a page to load after scanning a code, replace the prize draw with throwing a ball into a basket for a token, so the wait has something to watch. This proposal changes the activity if the venue approves it.

The two proposals change different objects, and the object is not a way to type anyone. Whether to change staffing or props depends on who has authority, how long approval takes, the fire requirement for the aisle, whether the props exist, and whether the temporary staff have practised; the same person in another role may propose the other option. ESTP will also draw up a staffing timetable, and ENTJ will also pick up a prop and change it; one change shows no stable difference.

### Why Ni and Se are shared while the judging pair swaps

In the common four-function notation used here, ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi and ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni. The two shared processes sit in different places: ENTJ has Ni second and Se third; ESTP has Se first and Ni last. The judging side swaps as a whole pair: Te and Fi against Ti and Fe.

Reading this pair through dominant and auxiliary is steadier: on the ENTJ side, judging more often lands in Te (externally checkable order, standards and resources), while perceiving is carried by Ni asking "what do these signals point to"; on the ESTP side, perceiving more often lands in Se (the observable facts in front of them), while judging is carried by Ti (whether this arrangement holds together internally). Ni and Se appear in both stacks under this convention. Their positions alone cannot show what either person will notice.

The attitude of the third process (Se for ENTJ, Fe for ESTP) may be marked introverted or extraverted in different sources, and some tables give only the function name without settling it. The disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early anyone moves; when a stack differs, check whether it states a version and a source. Position is emphasis inside the model, not a production sequence, and cannot be used to derive rescue steps, a division of work, or who is better to collaborate with. Both base pages are the [ENTJ profile](/en/personality/entj) and the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: what follows is one fictional exhibition floor and two fictional conversations. It covers communication and the organisation of information only, not handling procedures, and not fire evacuation, vehicle repair or contractual legal judgement. For a fire hazard, an injury, a vehicle stopped in traffic or an escalating contract dispute, contact site security and the fire service, or the local emergency or breakdown service, and follow the site lead, the professionals and the contract; organise information afterwards if there is capacity.

When the two work together, friction tends to appear over who authorises a change, who writes the trace, and how information is pooled. It is rarely a matter of who is right, but of which kind of information each takes first and how much authority each holds.

### Changing an interactive segment on the stand

(Fictional scene.) First morning of the fair, the plan was a scan-to-enter prize draw, the queue has blocked the main aisle, there is a media slot at eleven, the clear width follows the venue's fire requirements, the temporary staff arrived that morning, changes stay within authority, and anything beyond goes to venue approval.

One proposal closer to the ENTJ emphasis: estimate throughput per unit of time against the aisle width, release people in time slots, open two entrances, put one person at the end of the queue announcing the wait, and protect the media slot as a fixed point. One closer to the ESTP emphasis: find out why people are stuck, and if the bottleneck is a page loading after the scan, change the draw into throwing a ball into a basket for a token, turning the wait into something to watch.

Both remain proposals to be tested, so give them the same acceptance criteria first: whether the main aisle is passable again, whether throughput returns to threshold, whether waiting time falls. Only if there is a separate engagement goal do you look at how many people choose to stop and take part — and participation is never bought by sacrificing safe passage.

Write the failure signals too: whether time-slotted release holds the peak depends on whether people are "waiting too long" or "not knowing how long the wait is"; whether the new action can be sustained depends on how many props there are and whether the temporary staff have practised, otherwise the queue returns later. Being unable to state a revert condition only means this change has no agreed rollback yet; it does not mean the change is temporary, and it does not point to a type.

In the review, each writes three lines: what information was available, which standard was used to compare the two proposals, and which constraints decided the first step. The three lines are for checking information and judgement afterwards, not for typing by the object changed, the number of changes or the sequence.

### Two hours late with the stand builder

(Fictional scene.) The build is two hours late, the opening time does not move, the contract has a delay clause, the signatory is the project manager, and both can only speak within their own authority.

One opening closer to the ENTJ emphasis: put the contract clause, the construction schedule and tomorrow's must-finish point on the table, and ask first "which section can you finish by what time tomorrow", leaving responsibility and compensation until the schedule is confirmed. The gain is a checkable time point for progress; the risk is that the other side goes on the defensive and cooperation slows.

One opening closer to the ESTP emphasis: ask first which step is stuck, whether it is people or materials, then discuss "which part can we install first so the afternoon test run happens". The gain is real information from the floor and a temporary route; the risk is that responsibility and compensation get postponed if no separate time is set for them.

Either opening can obtain a schedule and either can fail to obtain compensation; the outcome depends on the contract terms, the other side's capacity to perform and the authority each holds, not on type. A workable division follows who can sign, who has read the contract and who knows the construction sequence, not type; in the same conversation, discussing progress and responsibility separately is usually clearer than mixing them. This is also a fictional case and guarantees no negotiation outcome.

### The car dies at the service area exit

(Fictional scene.) The car is safely parked away from moving traffic in a service area, and the travellers have contacted roadside assistance. They can share what they remember about the fault and discuss how the delay affects their trip. They leave recovery decisions to the operator and follow local safety guidance.

On that basis both do the same set of things, and differ only in which kind of information they are more likely to start from. One closer to the ENTJ emphasis: lay out the journey and the cost — how long recovery will take, how long towing to the nearest garage takes, where to stay tonight, how tomorrow's commitments shift. One closer to the ESTP emphasis: gather the car's current state and the known fault information — any unusual noise before it died, any warning on the dashboard, when it was last serviced, what was being done at the time.

These differences are closer to sourcing and outward arrangement (S/N and J/P), not to who is more willing to get their hands dirty. Either traveller can share information with the recovery service or update the itinerary. Who was driving, who has the relevant details and what the operator asks for determine how they divide the work.

Either preparation is worth writing and either is usable: one is "recovery arrives on time, what happens next", the other is "we cannot leave tonight, where do we stay and how does the itinerary change". These are contingency arrangements for anyone travelling together, not homework for one type; having only one of them means the other has not been written yet, not that one person handed the other possibility to someone else.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The first misread is treating "willing to decide on the spot" as evidence. Both types may settle it there and then, and both may ask first; how fast a decision comes depends on authority, consequences and how many people are present, and proves neither J nor P.

The second is treating hands-on as S and spreadsheets as N. ESTP will also write a review after the shift, and ENTJ will also carry boxes; neither action nor document is a criterion.

The third is treating "ignores process" as a trait of one type. Whether a process is followed depends more on whether it covers the current situation, how long approval takes and who carries the consequence; both types may follow it, and both may handle first and record afterwards within their authority.

The fourth is treating the object changed as the criterion. Whether staffing or props get changed is usually decided by role authority and the bottleneck at that moment; the same person in another role changes the other thing.

body: Scope note: what follows is one fictional exhibition floor and two fictional conversations. It covers communication and the organisation of information only, not handling procedures, and not fire evacuation, vehicle repair or contractual legal judgement. For a fire hazard, an injury, a vehicle stopped in traffic or an escalating contract dispute, contact site security and the fire service, or the local emergency or breakdown service, and follow the site lead, the professionals and the contract; organise information afterwards if there is capacity.

When the two work together, friction tends to appear over who authorises a change, who writes the trace, and how information is pooled. It is rarely a matter of who is right, but of which kind of information each takes first and how much authority each holds.

(Fictional scene.) First morning of the fair, the plan was a scan-to-enter prize draw, the queue has blocked the main aisle, there is a media slot at eleven, the clear width follows the venue's fire requirements, the temporary staff arrived that morning, changes stay within authority, and anything beyond goes to venue approval.

One closer to the ESTP emphasis: find out why people are stuck, and if the bottleneck is a page loading after the scan, change the draw into throwing a ball into a basket for a token, turning the wait into something to watch.

Both remain proposals to be tested, so give them the same acceptance criteria first: whether the main aisle is passable again, whether throughput returns to threshold, whether waiting time falls. Being unable to state a revert condition only means this change has no agreed rollback yet; it does not mean the change is temporary, and it does not point to a type.

In the review, each writes three lines: what information was available, which standard was used to compare the two proposals, and which constraints decided the first step. (Fictional scene.) The build is two hours late, the opening time does not move, the contract has a delay clause, the signatory is the project manager, and both can only speak within their own authority.

One opening closer to the ESTP emphasis: ask first which step is stuck, whether it is people or materials, then discuss "which part can we install first so the afternoon test run happens". This is also a fictional case and guarantees no negotiation outcome.

(Fictional scene.) The car is safely parked away from moving traffic in a service area, and the travellers have contacted roadside assistance. They can share what they remember about the fault and discuss how the delay affects their trip. They leave recovery decisions to the operator and follow local safety guidance.

items.answer:

items.answer:
Both types can do it; do not divide by type and do not judge competence by type.

body: In this fictional example, a queue blocks the main aisle on the first morning of a trade fair, and a media slot is scheduled for eleven. Two staff members are called to help. Both can stay engaged and follow the venue’s procedures. That response shows what they did in this situation.

The resemblance comes from the shared E and T: attention and energy turn more toward what is happening outside; and judgement more often wants a figure that can be put on the table and applied to everyone equally (throughput, waiting time, clear aisle width). That describes direction and standard, not who is more decisive, and not who understands the floor better.

The difference sits on two preferences. On sourcing, ENTJ more often takes the connections and direction of the information: where this queue will block in ten minutes, which step becomes the bottleneck first; ESTP more often takes the observable facts and past experience: which action people are stuck on right now, what happened last time this was changed. On the outward side, ENTJ more often settles the arrangement and the conclusion, and ESTP more often keeps options and adjusts while working.
### Changing the floor: resources or actions

The same fictional scene: the stand has pushed its queue into the main aisle, the aisle has to keep the clear width the fire rules require, there is a media slot at eleven, the temporary staff only arrived that morning, and both are proposing within their authority.

One proposal focuses on staffing and timing: estimate throughput per unit of time, release people in time slots, add a guiding position at the entrance, and put one person at the end of the queue to announce the expected wait. This proposal asks how many people can take part at a time, when to admit them and where to place staff.

Another proposal looks for a specific step that is slowing the queue: walk into the middle of the queue to see which step people are stuck on, and if the bottleneck is waiting for a page to load after scanning a code, replace the prize draw with throwing a ball into a basket for a token, so the wait has something to watch. This proposal changes the activity if the venue approves it.

The two proposals change different objects, and the object is not a way to type anyone. Whether to change staffing or props depends on who has authority, how long approval takes, the fire requirement for the aisle, whether the props exist, and whether the temporary staff have practised; the same person in another role may propose the other option. ESTP will also draw up a staffing timetable, and ENTJ will also pick up a prop and change it; one change shows no stable difference.

In the common four-function notation used here, ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi and ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni. The two shared processes sit in different places: ENTJ has Ni second and Se third; ESTP has Se first and Ni last. The judging side swaps as a whole pair: Te and Fi against Ti and Fe.

Reading this pair through dominant and auxiliary is steadier: on the ENTJ side, judging more often lands in Te (externally checkable order, standards and resources), while perceiving is carried by Ni asking "what do these signals point to"; on the ESTP side, perceiving more often lands in Se (the observable facts in front of them), while judging is carried by Ti (whether this arrangement holds together internally). Ni and Se appear in both stacks under this convention. Their positions alone cannot show what either person will notice.

The attitude of the third process (Se for ENTJ, Fe for ESTP) may be marked introverted or extraverted in different sources, and some tables give only the function name without settling it. comparison_public_projection_v1.summary:
ENTJ and ESTP share E and T and differ on S/N and J/P. Each difference has its own meaning, and neither can be flattened into "one plans, one rescues".

- E (Extraversion, shared): attention and energy turn more often toward the situation and the people outside; the opposite, I, turns more toward inner ideas and reactions. E describes direction, not social skill, not talkativeness, and not willingness to decide on the spot.
- T (Thinking, shared): judgement rests more often on impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently; the opposite, F, puts people and values into the judgement. T does not say who is calmer, and does not say who is less considerate.
- S/N: the ENTJ side, N, more often takes connections, patterns and possibility first; the ESTP side, S, more often takes observable facts and past experience first.
- J/P: the ENTJ side, J, more often forms outer arrangements and conclusions and turns open items into decisions; the ESTP side, P, more often keeps options so that new information can still rewrite the plan. This is about outward stance, and has nothing to do with efficiency, execution or the ability to carry a crisis.

Using the type-dynamics convention on this page, the stacks are: Te–Ni–Se–Fi for ENTJ and Se–Ti–Fe–Ni for ESTP. The two stacks share Ni and Se, and the judging side swaps as a pair, Te–Fi against Ti–Fe; the attitude of the third process (Se for ENTJ, Fe for ESTP) is labelled differently elsewhere, and this writing is a convention adopted here, not the Foundation's only version.

These describe emphasis inside the model. They do not predict the order of behaviour, who moves first, or who is better at rescuing a situation. Facing the same blocked aisle or the same delayed contract, either type may calculate first, ask first or start handling first; order is shaped more by role, duty, experience and conditions on the day.

sections.body_md:
In this fictional example, a queue blocks the main aisle on the first morning of a trade fair, and a media slot is scheduled for eleven. Two staff members are called to help. Both can stay engaged and follow the venue’s procedures. That response shows what they did in this situation.

The resemblance comes from the shared E and T: attention and energy turn more toward what is happening outside; and judgement more often wants a figure that can be put on the table and applied to everyone equally (throughput, waiting time, clear aisle width). That describes direction and standard, not who is more decisive, and not who understands the floor better.

The difference sits on two preferences. On sourcing, ENTJ more often takes the connections and direction of the information: where this queue will block in ten minutes, which step becomes the bottleneck first; ESTP more often takes the observable facts and past experience: which action people are stuck on right now, what happened last time this was changed. On the outward side, ENTJ more often settles the arrangement and the conclusion, and ESTP more often keeps options and adjusts while working.

### Changing the floor: resources or actions

The same fictional scene: the stand has pushed its queue into the main aisle, the aisle has to keep the clear width the fire rules require, there is a media slot at eleven, the temporary staff only arrived that morning, and both are proposing within their authority.

One proposal focuses on staffing and timing: estimate throughput per unit of time, release people in time slots, add a guiding position at the entrance, and put one person at the end of the queue to announce the expected wait. This proposal asks how many people can take part at a time, when to admit them and where to place staff.

Another proposal looks for a specific step that is slowing the queue: walk into the middle of the queue to see which step people are stuck on, and if the bottleneck is waiting for a page to load after scanning a code, replace the prize draw with throwing a ball into a basket for a token, so the wait has something to watch. This proposal changes the activity if the venue approves it.

The two proposals change different objects, and the object is not a way to type anyone. Whether to change staffing or props depends on who has authority, how long approval takes, the fire requirement for the aisle, whether the props exist, and whether the temporary staff have practised; the same person in another role may propose the other option. ESTP will also draw up a staffing timetable, and ENTJ will also pick up a prop and change it; one change shows no stable difference.

### Why Ni and Se are shared while the judging pair swaps

In the common four-function notation used here, ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi and ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni. The two shared processes sit in different places: ENTJ has Ni second and Se third; ESTP has Se first and Ni last. The judging side swaps as a whole pair: Te and Fi against Ti and Fe.

Reading this pair through dominant and auxiliary is steadier: on the ENTJ side, judging more often lands in Te (externally checkable order, standards and resources), while perceiving is carried by Ni asking "what do these signals point to"; on the ESTP side, perceiving more often lands in Se (the observable facts in front of them), while judging is carried by Ti (whether this arrangement holds together internally). Ni and Se appear in both stacks under this convention. Their positions alone cannot show what either person will notice.

The attitude of the third process (Se for ENTJ, Fe for ESTP) may be marked introverted or extraverted in different sources, and some tables give only the function name without settling it. The disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early anyone moves; when a stack differs, check whether it states a version and a source. Position is emphasis inside the model, not a production sequence, and cannot be used to derive rescue steps, a division of work, or who is better to collaborate with. Both base pages are the [ENTJ profile](/en/personality/entj) and the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp).

Scope note: what follows is one fictional exhibition floor and two fictional conversations. It covers communication and the organisation of information only, not handling procedures, and not fire evacuation, vehicle repair or contractual legal judgement. For a fire hazard, an injury, a vehicle stopped in traffic or an escalating contract dispute, contact site security and the fire service, or the local emergency or breakdown service, and follow the site lead, the professionals and the contract; organise information afterwards if there is capacity.

When the two work together, friction tends to appear over who authorises a change, who writes the trace, and how information is pooled. It is rarely a matter of who is right, but of which kind of information each takes first and how much authority each holds.

### Changing an interactive segment on the stand

(Fictional scene.) First morning of the fair, the plan was a scan-to-enter prize draw, the queue has blocked the main aisle, there is a media slot at eleven, the clear width follows the venue's fire requirements, the temporary staff arrived that morning, changes stay within authority, and anything beyond goes to venue approval.

One proposal closer to the ENTJ emphasis: estimate throughput per unit of time against the aisle width, release people in time slots, open two entrances, put one person at the end of the queue announcing the wait, and protect the media slot as a fixed point. One closer to the ESTP emphasis: find out why people are stuck, and if the bottleneck is a page loading after the scan, change the draw into throwing a ball into a basket for a token, turning the wait into something to watch.

Both remain proposals to be tested, so give them the same acceptance criteria first: whether the main aisle is passable again, whether throughput returns to threshold, whether waiting time falls. Only if there is a separate engagement goal do you look at how many people choose to stop and take part — and participation is never bought by sacrificing safe passage.

Write the failure signals too: whether time-slotted release holds the peak depends on whether people are "waiting too long" or "not knowing how long the wait is"; whether the new action can be sustained depends on how many props there are and whether the temporary staff have practised, otherwise the queue returns later. Being unable to state a revert condition only means this change has no agreed rollback yet; it does not mean the change is temporary, and it does not point to a type.

In the review, each writes three lines: what information was available, which standard was used to compare the two proposals, and which constraints decided the first step. The three lines are for checking information and judgement afterwards, not for typing by the object changed, the number of changes or the sequence.

### Two hours late with the stand builder

(Fictional scene.) The build is two hours late, the opening time does not move, the contract has a delay clause, the signatory is the project manager, and both can only speak within their own authority.

One opening closer to the ENTJ emphasis: put the contract clause, the construction schedule and tomorrow's must-finish point on the table, and ask first "which section can you finish by what time tomorrow", leaving responsibility and compensation until the schedule is confirmed. The gain is a checkable time point for progress; the risk is that the other side goes on the defensive and cooperation slows.

One opening closer to the ESTP emphasis: ask first which step is stuck, whether it is people or materials, then discuss "which part can we install first so the afternoon test run happens". The gain is real information from the floor and a temporary route; the risk is that responsibility and compensation get postponed if no separate time is set for them.

Either opening can obtain a schedule and either can fail to obtain compensation; the outcome depends on the contract terms, the other side's capacity to perform and the authority each holds, not on type. A workable division follows who can sign, who has read the contract and who knows the construction sequence, not type; in the same conversation, discussing progress and responsibility separately is usually clearer than mixing them. This is also a fictional case and guarantees no negotiation outcome.

### The car dies at the service area exit

(Fictional scene.) The car is safely parked away from moving traffic in a service area, and the travellers have contacted roadside assistance. They can share what they remember about the fault and discuss how the delay affects their trip. They leave recovery decisions to the operator and follow local safety guidance.

On that basis both do the same set of things, and differ only in which kind of information they are more likely to start from. One closer to the ENTJ emphasis: lay out the journey and the cost — how long recovery will take, how long towing to the nearest garage takes, where to stay tonight, how tomorrow's commitments shift. One closer to the ESTP emphasis: gather the car's current state and the known fault information — any unusual noise before it died, any warning on the dashboard, when it was last serviced, what was being done at the time.

These differences are closer to sourcing and outward arrangement (S/N and J/P), not to who is more willing to get their hands dirty. Either traveller can share information with the recovery service or update the itinerary. Who was driving, who has the relevant details and what the operator asks for determine how they divide the work.

Either preparation is worth writing and either is usable: one is "recovery arrives on time, what happens next", the other is "we cannot leave tonight, where do we stay and how does the itinerary change". These are contingency arrangements for anyone travelling together, not homework for one type; having only one of them means the other has not been written yet, not that one person handed the other possibility to someone else.
